title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Refineries | MPI, US
description: On-site MPI for US refinery vessels, piping, tanks and lifting lugs: sour-service, caustic and repair welds. Send your weld list and request an MT quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Refineries: Weld Cracking and Repair Checks
html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to US refineries to perform magnetic particle inspection (MPI, or mag particle testing) on carbon and low-alloy steel welds and components. We look for cracks that break the surface or sit just beneath it: nozzle and attachment welds on vessels, piping repair welds, storage tank shell and roof welds, lifting lugs and structural steel. Findings go to the owner's inspector for disposition. Request an MT inspection quote and send your weld list.

Why MT earns its place on refinery steel

Most pressure-retaining steel in a refinery is ferromagnetic, which means a magnetic field can be driven through it and a crack that interrupts the field draws iron particles to itself. That is the entire principle. It is fast, it is sensitive to tight cracks that visual examination misses, and it needs less surface preparation than most alternatives. The method fails on austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, which do not carry a magnetic field, so those parts go to the penetrant method instead; liquid penetrant testing for refineries covers that side.

The refinery's own risk framework explains where MT gets used. API 571 lists the cracking mechanisms to watch, API 510 and API 570 call for examination after repair and alteration, and API 653 sets expectations for tank welds. The owner's inspector chooses which welds need surface examination; we perform it and report.

Cracking mechanisms MT is asked to find

  • Wet hydrogen sulfide cracking. Sulfide stress cracking and stress-oriented cracking appear at or beside welds in sour service on vessels and piping in sour water, amine, hydroprocessing and fractionator overhead systems. Hard heat-affected zones are the usual starting point, so fluorescent wet particle examination at welds is common after shutdowns.
  • Caustic and amine stress corrosion cracking. Carbon steel welds in caustic treating and amine systems can crack where residual stress was never relieved. These cracks tend to run parallel to the weld and are good MT targets.
  • Carbonate cracking. Alkaline sour water in FCC wet gas and main fractionator overhead service can crack carbon steel welds, again along the heat-affected zone.
  • Fatigue. Vibrating small-bore connections, branch welds and supports crack at the weld toe. A quick MT pass on a branch weld after a vibration complaint is routine.
  • Weld repairs. Excavations of defects are examined by MT before welding and again on the finished weld, per the repair procedure.

The scope on any job comes from the owner's damage-mechanism review. We do not pick locations; we examine what the inspector marks and report what we find, including where we were unable to examine because of access or geometry.

Technique details for refinery conditions

  • Yoke method. An alternating-current yoke with articulated legs is the field standard for welds, set up per ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709. The lift capacity of the yoke is verified at the start of each shift and recorded.
  • Two directions. Cracks run in any direction, so each area is examined twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees. A single pass misses cracks parallel to the field.
  • Dry or wet particles. Dry powder suits warm surfaces and rough weld profiles; wet particles in suspension, often fluorescent and viewed under ultraviolet light in a darkened area, suit tight cracks and are the usual choice for sour service.
  • Light levels. Visible-light examinations require a minimum light level at the part, measured with a calibrated meter. Fluorescent work requires a measured ultraviolet intensity and a dark enough area.
  • Surface condition. Heavy scale, weld spatter and thick coatings reduce sensitivity. The procedure states how much coating is acceptable; beyond that, the owner's crew removes it first.
  • Temperature. Fluids and particles have temperature limits. Hot surfaces may need dry powder or a special procedure qualified for the temperature in question.
  • Prods and ignition. Electrical prods can arc, so prod magnetization in classified areas needs the owner's hot work permit or is replaced by a yoke.

Weld repair workflow, step by step

A repair is where MT is used most deliberately, and the sequence matters. First the defect is excavated by grinding; MT confirms the crack is fully gone before any welding starts, because welding over a remnant simply buries it. After welding, the repair is ground flush if the procedure requires it and examined again. If preheat or postweld heat treatment applies, the owner decides whether the final examination happens before or after, and we ask for that sequence in writing so the surface condition is right when we arrive.

Each pass leaves a record. Reports list the excavation examination and the final examination separately, so the inspector can see that the repair was checked twice. When a crack keeps reappearing after repair, that is useful information for the owner's engineer, who may suspect a mechanism that welding alone will not fix.

Demagnetization, cleaning and leaving the equipment as found

A magnetized part can distort later weld arcs and can hold iron particles against its surface. Where the procedure requires it, we check residual field and demagnetize, and we remove the particles and suspension afterward, since leftover carrier can affect coatings or linger in a small crevice. Wet particle suspension is oil or water based; the procedure and the site's waste rules decide where wipe-up rags and spent fluid go. These details are small but they separate a tidy shutdown inspection from one that leaves work behind for the paint crew.

When another method is a better choice

Magnetic particle inspection tells you nothing about wall loss, so a corroded line needs ultrasonic testing for refineries instead. It also cannot see flaws that sit deep inside a thick weld. On stainless overlay, 300-series piping or alloy cladding, switch to penetrant. A thorough weld inspection often combines methods; the MT versus PT guide walks through the decision, and the complete MT guide covers the physics. For the weld context, see weld inspection services.

Limits of the method on refinery equipment

Three limits come up repeatedly. First, sensitivity falls off with depth, so a crack buried a quarter inch below the surface may not produce an indication at all. Second, geometry matters: sharp internal corners, thread roots and tight fillet junctions hold particles in ways that look like indications and are not, so the technician has to recognize non-relevant patterns and record them honestly. Third, a field has to reach the crack at a useful angle, and a heavy casting or complex nozzle may need more than one yoke position. When we cannot examine an area properly, the report says so rather than implying a clean result.

Acceptance: who decides and against what

Acceptance criteria come from the construction or repair code, usually ASME B31.3 for process piping and ASME Section VIII for vessels, with Section V Article 7 governing how the examination is performed. For tanks, API 653 and the standard the tank was built to apply. Rounded indications and linear indications are judged differently, and any crack is rejected. The technician reports; the owner's inspector accepts, rejects or orders repair. We record the criteria cited on the report so the disposition is traceable.

Planning for a refinery shutdown

Mag particle work sits late in many turnaround schedules because it follows grinding, weld repair and surface cleaning. Share the sequence so our crew is mobilized when the surfaces are actually ready. In the United States, refinery sites require safety orientation, permits, gas testing and, near ports, TWIC. Fluorescent MT needs a dark enclosure or shade, which can be hard to set up in the open sun or beside live equipment; tell us the work location. Scaffold and rope access are set by the site. The turnaround and shutdown page explains how we fit into an outage.

What the MT report contains

  • Equipment and weld identification, tied to the owner's weld map or isometric.
  • Procedure number and revision, and the code section governing examination and acceptance.
  • Yoke or equipment ID, lift test results and particle type, color and brand lot.
  • Light-meter or ultraviolet-meter readings for the examination area.
  • Technician name and level, and the ASNT Level III who approved the procedure and reviewed the report.
  • Indications with position, length and type, a sketch, and accept or reject against the cited criteria.
  • Areas not examined, with the reason.

What to send us for a quote

  • Weld list, weld map or drawings with equipment tags.
  • Base metal and thickness, and whether welds are in sour, caustic or amine service.
  • Quantity of welds or linear feet and the code or specification invoked.
  • Surface condition, coating, insulation and temperature of each area.
  • Access, light conditions and any darkened area you can provide.
  • Site address, badging and safety orientation, and your turnaround dates.

Where we work in the US for refining

  • Houston: the Ship Channel refineries and their turnaround workforce.
  • Beaumont: Southeast Texas refineries that run sour and heavy crude units.
  • Baton Rouge: the river refining corridor of south Louisiana.
  • Lake Charles: western Louisiana refining on the Calcasieu channel.
  • Corpus Christi: South Texas refineries and tank terminals.
  • Tulsa: Oklahoma refining and the pipeline hub nearby.
  • Salt Lake City: Rocky Mountain refineries on waxy crudes.
  • Toledo: Great Lakes refining and chemical plants.

Training your own technicians

Companies that want in-house MT capability can use MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training with the magnetic particle simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own people, so a technical procedure and written practice come first. Programs for the sector are outlined on the oil and gas NDT training page. For ultrasonic or penetrant needs at the same site, see the national magnetic particle testing page.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. We do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not act as the authorized inspector of record; that is the owner's role. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be used on stainless steel piping in a refinery?
faq.a: Not on austenitic stainless, which is not ferromagnetic. Ferritic and martensitic grades and carbon steel respond, but 300-series piping and nickel alloys need liquid penetrant instead.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MT on refinery welds?
faq.a: A weld list or map, base metal and thickness, quantity, the governing code, surface and coating condition, temperature, access and your outage dates. Service type (sour, caustic, amine) also helps us choose dry or fluorescent wet particles.
The owner's inspector does, against the code in the procedure. Our technician reports the indication with position, length and type, and the report records the acceptance criteria that were cited.

faq.q: Is fluorescent MT better than visible MT?
faq.a: Fluorescent wet particles show tight cracks more clearly, so they suit sour-service welds, but they need a dark area and ultraviolet lamp. Visible dry or wet color-contrast particles are simpler in bright, open work areas.

faq.q: Do you need to remove paint before MT?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded coatings may be acceptable if the procedure was qualified for them. Thick or flaking coatings, scale and spatter should be removed, because they weaken the indication and hide cracks.

faq.q: Can MT find corrosion or wall loss?
faq.a: No. It finds surface and near-surface cracks. For thickness and corrosion surveys we use ultrasonic testing, often in the same mobilization as the weld examination.

faq.q: Is magnetic particle work safe near live equipment?
faq.a: Yokes do not need open arcing, but prods can. The site's permit system decides, and in classified areas we use the yoke method or wait for the right permit.

faq.q: Can you do tank welds as well as vessels and piping?
faq.a: Yes. Tank shell, bottom and roof welds are routine MT targets, and the owner's API 653 inspector decides which are examined. Atlantis supplies the examination data only.

faq.q: Do your technicians travel outside the Gulf Coast?
faq.a: Yes. They mobilize to refineries anywhere in the United States. Smaller or remote sites need more lead time for travel and credentials, so share the dates early.
